newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN names first rights investigator on Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: UN names first rights investigator on Nigeria.

text.p: A southern African law professor was chosen on Tuesday to investigate human rights in Nigeria for the United Nations.

Tiyanjana Maluwa of the University of Cape Town, South Africa, would be the U.N. Human Rights Commission's first special rapporteur to probe allegations of major abuses in Nigeria, including executions. He holds Malawi nationality
Michel Moussalli, a Swiss who worked nearly 20 years for the U.N. refugee agency, was nominated as the commission's special representative on Rwanda.
The nominations were made by the Czech diplomat Miroslav Somol, who served as chairman of the 1997 Commission, and announced in a U.N. statement.

The 53-member commission agreed in April to name an investigator for Nigeria and called on the Lagos government to guarantee fundamental freedoms and release "all prisoners, trade union leaders, human rights advocates and journalists currently detained".

Nigeria drew international condemnation in November 1995 when it hanged Ken Saro Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Other jailed Ogonis currently face the death penalty on the same murder charges, U.N. sources say.
In April, Rwanda successfully lobbied for the Commission not to renew the mandate of the special rapporteur to its country where half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates were killed in 1994.
Instead, it agreed to name a "special representative" for Rwanda who is expected to have less of an investigative role and more of a brief to oversee U.N. technical advisory services.
Their mandates have to be approved by the U.N. Economic and Social Council which holds talks in Geneva next week, according to the U.N. statement.
"The appointments are the chairman's decision and ECOSOC usually rubber-stamps the mandates," a U.N. source said.
